title: A field guide to alpine photography
transcript: Alpine photography starts before the summit catches light. I walk the ridge in blue hour and choose one camera position while the valley is still in shadow. For alpine photography, side light is the first thing I look for. Side light catches the limestone edges while the rock behind them stays dark. A long lens helps separate one ridge from the next. I keep the nearest pine trees in the frame so the layers have a sense of scale. Watch the low cloud. When low cloud moves through the valley, the middle ridge disappears for a moment and the outline of the summit becomes cleaner. Once the side light reaches the highest peak, I check the histogram. I lower the exposure just enough to hold detail in the brightest patch of limestone. Before I leave, I make one wider frame. Alpine photography rewards waiting. A long lens describes the mountain, but the wider view shows what the morning felt like.
